title: In-Situ Polarimetry in Collimated Magneto-Infrared Spectroscopy System
authors: Zeping Shi, Wenbin Wu, Zhiwei Zhang, Yuhan Du, Chenyao Xu, Congming Hao, Xiangyu Jiang, Xin Chen, Guangyi Wang, Mingsen Zhou, Chunhui Pan, Wei Lu, Hao Shen, Haifeng Pan, Zhenrong Sun, Junhao Chu, Xiang Yuan
abstract: Magneto-infrared spectroscopy under strong magnetic fields provides a powerful probe of Landau quantization and field-induced collective excitations, yet its full potential has long been constrained by the lack of in-situ polarization control, because the highly divergent infrared beam propagating through narrow light tubes undergoes multiple wall reflections, leading to severe polarization degradation. Here we report a collimated magneto-infrared spectroscopy system that integrates continuous in-situ polarimetry. The system employs incident and exit collimation chambers forming a Kepler type optical architecture, which converts the large-aperture FTIR output into a low-divergence beam and strongly suppresses multi-reflection trajectories inside long gold-plated light tubes, thereby enhancing both optical throughput and polarization fidelity. A remotely controlled polarization module, consisting of an automated linear polarizer and a switchable Fresnel rhomb positioned entirely outside the high-field region, enables continuous in-situ tuning between linear, circular, and arbitrary elliptical polarization states without thermal cycling, manual realignment, or breaking vacuum. Interchangeable compact focusing modules further support Faraday and Voigt geometries in both transmission and reflection experiments within a 50 mm magnet bore, providing efficient beam focusing and signal collection while maintaining polarization fidelity. The setup achieves a minimum root-mean-square noise of 0.0033%, an average noise of 0.0082%, and a linear polarization extinction ratio up to 40:1. We demonstrate the capability through continuous in-situ linear polarimetry and broadband circular polarimetry in the magneto-infrared spectroscopy of various single crystals. This platform establishes a robust experimental framework for in-situ polarization-resolved magneto-infrared spectroscopy.
summary: This paper introduces an advanced magneto-infrared spectroscopy system designed to overcome polarization degradation caused by light beam reflections in high-field environments. By implementing a collimated optical architecture and placing the polarization module outside the magnet bore, the setup achieves superior polarization fidelity and low noise floors. This platform enables sensitive, continuous measurements of magnetic field effects on material optical properties via linear and circular polarimetry.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving high-fidelity, continuous in-situ polarization control for magneto-infrared spectroscopy measurements performed within strong magnetic fields.
main_result: The authors report a novel collimated system that successfully integrates remote polarization modules and multiple interchangeable focusing optics, enabling robust polarization-resolved measurements across various geometries.
method: The methodology involves redesigning the optical path using Kepler type telescopes to collimate the FTIR beam, thereby suppressing detrimental multi-wall reflections in long light tubes. Polarization control is achieved externally via automated polarizers and Fresnel rhombs.
model_or_system: The system is a complex magneto-infrared spectroscopy platform featuring incident/exit collimation chambers, interchangeable focusing modules for Faraday/Voigt geometries (transmission/reflection), and an external polarization module operating under vacuum conditions. It operates within a superconducting magnet bore up to 50 mm.
key_observables: Linear polarization extinction ratio (up to 40:1), minimum root-mean-square noise ($\le 0.0033\%$), relative transmission/reflectivity spectra as a function of magnetic field and polarization angle.
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength (up to 12 T), sample bore size ($\sim 50 	ext{ mm}$), spectral range (broadband, VIS to FIR).
main_assumptions: The collimation design successfully suppresses higher-order wall reflections compared to conventional direct focusing schemes. The polarization module is placed outside the high-field region to maintain functionality.
figures_summary: Figures detail the overall system schematic (Fig. 1), incident/exit collimation optics (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), the in-situ polarization module setup (Fig. 4), and the four interchangeable magneto-infrared focusing modules supporting various geometries (Faraday/Voigt transmission/reflection) (Fig. 5).
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the scientific need for polarization control, details the optical engineering solution (collimation architecture), describes the modular hardware implementation (polarization module and focusing optics), and finally demonstrates its capability through measurements of linear and circular polarimetry on single crystals.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum information theory, this work represents a significant advancement in experimental quantum optics instrumentation. The ability to perform polarization-resolved spectroscopy *in situ* under extreme conditions (high B-field, vacuum) is crucial for probing fundamental quantum phenomena like Landau quantization and magnetic circular dichroism.
